title: A basket on the Nile (Exodus 2:1–10)
hookLine: Yocheved hides her baby, Miriam watches, Pharaoh's daughter draws him out

cards: If you've ever had a newborn in the house, you know: they're not quiet. They cry at three in the morning. They cry when you're trying to be invisible.

Now imagine hiding one, in a country where soldiers are looking for baby boys. A woman from the tribe of Levi gives birth to a son. She sees that he's good, the text says, and she hides him for three months.
Then she can't anymore. So she makes a decision no parent should ever have to make.

teach.h: TEVAH: THE SAME WORD AS NOAH'S ARK.
teach.b: She takes an ark of bulrushes, waterproofs it with pitch, puts the baby inside, and sets it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile.
The Hebrew word for this little basket is tevah, the same word used for Noah's ark, and nowhere else in the Torah. Once, a box on the water saved all of life. Now a box on the water carries one baby.
Then a small, enormous detail: "And his sister stood afar off, to know what would be done to him." She isn't named here, but later we learn: Miriam. A young girl, hiding in the reeds, watching.
Pharaoh's own daughter comes down to bathe. She sees the basket, opens it, and the baby is crying. She has compassion on him.
She knows exactly what this is: one of the Hebrews' children. The daughter of the man who ordered the boys drowned decides to save one. Now Miriam moves.
She steps out of the reeds: shall I go and find you a Hebrew woman to nurse the baby for you? Go, says the princess.

teach.h: HIS MOTHER, PAID TO NURSE HIM.
teach.b: Miriam runs and brings the baby's own mother, Yocheved, as the text later names her, and now she's being paid to nurse her own son.

teach.h: I DREW HIM OUT OF THE WATER.
teach.b: When he's older, she brings him back to the palace, and Pharaoh's daughter names him Moshe, Moses: "Because I drew him out of the water." Three women.
A mother who let go, a sister who watched, and a princess who broke her father's law. The rabbis give that princess a name: Bityah, daughter of God.

how: Jewish tradition honors the women of the Exodus story, Yocheved, Miriam, the midwives and Pharaoh's daughter, whom the rabbis call Bityah, and teaches that Israel was redeemed from Egypt in the merit of righteous women.

games.q: you're Miriam, hiding in the reeds. Pharaoh's daughter has just opened the basket and is holding your crying baby brother. what do you do?
o: step out and offer to find a Hebrew nurse.
run home and tell your mother.
games.why: she steps out and offers to find a nurse, and brings the baby's own mother. a girl's quick courage keeps the family together.

practice: Think of someone you can't protect directly right now: a grown child on their own, a friend facing something they have to face themselves, a parent far away.
You can't carry them, but you can watch, holding them in mind the way Miriam stood in the reeds. If you pray, you can pray for them, and think of one small way to let them know someone's watching.
